subject: Macklem defends the hike into a soft job market
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a variable-rate mortgage or a job you are not fully sure about, Tuesday was the Bank of Canada telling you it is not done raising rates. Governor Tiff Macklem spent the afternoon in front of the House of Commons finance committee defending a hike he made a week earlier, in an economy he himself described as having more supply than demand.

## What Macklem actually said

The Bank raised its policy rate a quarter point to 2.5 per cent on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, and on Tuesday Macklem went to Parliament to explain why. BNN Bloomberg reported that he told MPs the main force pushing Canadian inflation higher right now is the global energy shock from the war in the Middle East, and that there could be a need to raise rates again. He also said the economy is in **excess supply**, meaning businesses can produce more than Canadians are currently buying. Read those two statements together and you get something strange. A central bank normally cuts when there is slack in the economy. Macklem is tightening anyway, because he is worried about what happens when expensive fuel works its way into bus fares, groceries, restaurant menus and eventually wage demands.

## The gasoline problem

Statistics Canada's September numbers, released October 19, show the shape of his problem. Headline inflation was 3.1 per cent, up from 3.0 per cent in August, and gasoline on its own was up 27.8 per cent from a year earlier, against 22.8 per cent in August. Take gasoline out and inflation was 2.2 per cent, down from 2.4. All three of the Bank's preferred core measures, which throw out the noisiest prices to find the underlying trend, got cooler, not hotter: CPI-trim at 1.8 per cent, CPI-median at 1.9, CPI-common at 2.4. So the trend underneath is at or below target and one volatile line is doing the damage. My view is that this is a thin case for a hike. Macklem's answer is that he cannot know in advance whether an oil shock stays in one line of the index or leaks into everything else, and he would rather move early than apologize in 2028.

## What I am watching Thursday and Friday

The testimony was the warm-up. CBC News reported that Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne will table the federal budget tomorrow, and the Parliamentary Budget Officer already projects a deficit of $63.3 billion for 2026-27 climbing to $70.2 billion in 2027-28, with real GDP growth of only 0.9 per cent this year. Macklem told MPs that federal fiscal policy is not making his inflation fight harder, which is a very careful thing to say two days before a budget. Then on Friday at 8:30 a.m. Eastern, Statistics Canada publishes the Labour Force Survey. Macklem has said unemployment has sat near 6.5 per cent for several months. If Friday's number breaks above that, the Bank is raising rates into a labour market that is visibly cracking, and the next decision gets much harder to read.

## The takeaway

If you are renewing a mortgage in the next few months, price the fixed option as though 2.5 per cent is a floor rather than a ceiling, because Macklem has now signalled twice in eight days that he may go again. Watch the gasoline line in the next CPI release more closely than the headline, since that one line is doing all of the work. Watch whether tomorrow's budget leans on capital spending to keep the operating side balanced, because that definition is what lets Ottawa spend heavily without breaking its own fiscal rule. Honestly, I care less about what the Bank does in December than about whether 6.5 per cent unemployment holds on Friday.
